Reformed
rih-FORMD
adjective; noun (collective)
From Latin reformare (“to form again, to restore”) — re- (“again”) + formare (“to form, to shape”); adopted in the sixteenth century to designate the theological tradition descending from Zwingli, Calvin, Bucer, Beza, and the English and Scottish Reformers that structured its confession around the sovereignty of God, the covenant of grace, and sola Scriptura.

Biblical Definition

The word “Reformed” in Christian usage identifies the confessionally Calvinist wing of the Protestant Reformation — the theological tradition that crystallized in the German and Swiss Reformed churches, the Dutch Three-Forms-of-Unity churches, and the Anglo-Scottish Presbyterian and English Reformed Baptist lines. It is distinguished from the Lutheran tradition by its covenant theology (law-gospel continuity through the covenants of works and grace), its doctrine of the Lord's Supper (spiritual presence by faith rather than Lutheran sacramental union), its regulative principle of worship (what Scripture does not command is not permitted in corporate worship), and its fuller development of the sovereignty of God in election, definite atonement, and effectual calling. The Berean standard of examining the Scriptures daily (Acts 17:11) and the Reformation cry “to the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20) both express the Reformed instinct: all doctrine and practice measured by Scripture alone. Reformed theology is not a party label but a theological posture — God's Word governs both what is believed and how it is worshipped, and every received tradition remains subject to continual reformation by that Word. The great confessional standards — the Westminster Confession (1646), the Three Forms of Unity (Heidelberg, Belgic, Canons of Dort), and the 1689 London Baptist Confession — express this posture in its mature doctrinal form, and together constitute the confessional Reformed family. “The law of the LORD is perfect, converting the soul: the testimony of the LORD is sure, making wise the simple.” (Ps 19:7) — Scripture's sufficiency for life and doctrine is the Reformed tradition's enduring conviction.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) gives “reformed” as the past participle of “reform,” meaning corrected from error or amended; in ecclesiastical use it designates the confessionally Calvinist Protestant churches that took their stand on Scripture alone against medieval accretions.

expand to see more

REFORMED, pp. [L. reformatus.] 1. Corrected; amended; restored to a former good state; or changed from a worse to a better state. 2. Protestant; specifically applied to those who embraced the doctrines of the Reformation, particularly the Calvinist or Zwinglian branch of the Protestant movement, as distinguished from the Lutheran.

REFORMED CHURCHES. Those Protestant churches which follow the theological tradition established by Zwingli, Calvin, Beza, and the Synod of Dort — confessionally committed to the sovereignty of God in salvation, the covenant framework of Scripture, the regulative principle of worship, and the five points of Calvinist soteriology.

The word distinguishes the Genevan tradition (Calvin, Knox, Bucer) from the Wittenberg tradition (Luther, Melanchthon) on sacramental theology and ecclesiology, while uniting both as children of the one Reformation recovery of the apostolic gospel against Roman accretion.

Modern Corruption

The label “Reformed” has been stretched to cover any Protestant church retaining loose Reformation heritage; within confessional circles, Radical Two-Kingdoms theology and Federal Vision have been distinct internal drift movements.

expand to see more

In popular evangelical usage, “Reformed” has been reduced to a synonym for “Calvinist soteriology,” stripped of its ecclesiological, liturgical, and confessional freight. Churches that adopt five-point Calvinist soteriology while practicing contemporary worship without confessional discipline often call themselves “Reformed” — but the historical tradition requires far more: covenant theology, the regulative principle of worship, confessional subscription, and ordered church government. The reduction of Reformed to a soteriology-only label both flatters its holders and cheapens the tradition they claim to inhabit.

Within confessional Reformed circles, two drift movements deserve naming. Radical Two-Kingdoms theology (associated with Darryl Hart and earlier Michael Horton) so separates the sacred and secular spheres that Christ's lordship over public life is effectively withdrawn — a position the Westminster Confession (ch. 23) and 1689 LBCF (ch. 24) resist. Federal Vision theology (Norman Shepherd, Peter Leithart, James Jordan) reintroduced works-conditionality into the covenant of grace, blurring justification by faith alone in a way that multiple Presbyterian and Reformed presbyteries formally condemned. The Reformed tradition is not self-immunized against drift; it is semper reformanda (“always being reformed”) by the same Word that founded it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Rooted in Latin reformare (“to form again”) and the sixteenth-century confessional theology of Geneva, Zurich, Strasbourg, and the Dutch and British Reformations — the tradition that produced the Westminster Confession, the Three Forms of Unity, and the 1689 London Baptist Confession.

expand to see more

Latin reformare — to form again, to restore; root of ‘Reformation,’ ‘reform,’ and ‘Reformed’ — all pointing to correction by return to an original standard, namely the apostolic Scripture

Latin semper reformanda — always being reformed; the Reformed tradition's motto in its full form: ecclesia reformata, semper reformanda secundum verbum Dei — a church reformed and always reforming according to the Word of God

Synod of Dort (1618–1619) — the landmark Dutch Reformed council that codified the five Calvinist responses to Arminianism (the Canons of Dort), establishing the doctrinal boundaries of confessional Reformed soteriology for the continental tradition

Three Forms of Unity — the Heidelberg Catechism (1563), Belgic Confession (1561), and Canons of Dort (1619) — the doctrinal standards of the continental Reformed tradition, parallel to the Westminster Standards in the Anglo-Scottish line

1689 London Baptist Confession — the Reformed Baptist articulation of the same tradition, following the Westminster Confession closely except on baptism (believer's by immersion), ecclesiology (congregational), and civil magistrate, making it the dictionary's primary confessional anchor

Usage

"The Reformed tradition is defined not by a single theologian but by a family of confessions: a church is Reformed in proportion to its subscription to the Westminster Standards or the Three Forms of Unity and its practice of the regulative principle — not merely by its soteriology."

"The Berean instinct (Acts 17:11) — examining the Scriptures daily to test all teaching — is the epistemological posture that the Reformed tradition institutionalizes in its confessional system: no teacher, no tradition, and no experience stands above Scripture's verdict."

"“Reformed and always reforming according to the Word of God” is not a permission slip for innovation; the full phrase insists that reformation is always secundum verbum Dei — according to the Word — a check against both stagnant conservatism and restless novelty disguised as prophetic courage."
